video_title: What Robert Caro learned about power after studying it for 50 years
transcript: "If you do everything, you will win." That is the maxim by which Lyndon   Johnson lived his life. My guest today is Robert Caro.  Over the 50 years that he has spent writing  about Lyndon Johnson, he has lived in the   edges of the Texas Hill Country to understand  the poverty and loneliness of Johnson’s youth.  He has sifted through millions of documents  in the Senate and presidential libraries   of the entire nation. He has chased down for   interviews everyone, from the former goon who  helped Johnson steal an election to the chauffeur   who drove him on his first desperate campaign. In other words, my guest today is a man   who understands Johnson’s aphorism:  "If you do everything, you’ll win."  Mr. Caro, it is such a huge  honor to have you on the show.  It’s great to be here. My first question is what   I hinted at in the introduction. How much do you see yourself   represented in Johnson or in Moses? Is part of the reason you’re able to   write so compellingly about them that  you share some of their qualities?  Let me say first, I think, I hope, there are  qualities of both these guys that I don’t share.  Among other things they’re so,  I’ll use the word, ruthless.  You say they’d do anything to win. That’s part of their greatness.  I remember when I started learning about  Robert Moses, I went to the La Guardia   papers, which were kept in the Boat Basin. They were stored by the Municipal Archives,   literally in the 79th Street Boat Basin  on the Hudson River, three levels down.  There was this row of file  cabinets against the wall.  I’m sitting there day after day  going through these documents.  Occasionally I’d come across a note that  Robert Moses wrote, and I realized I’m   following the same path he was. It’s fascinating, actually.  Obviously, not all the qualities. But the quality I’m referring to   here is that just like Johnson or just like  Moses, you refuse to take no for an answer.  If somebody says, "I won’t give you  an interview," you don’t stop there.  You refuse to leave a stone unturned. So there is a relentlessness that   you share with these subjects. I’m going to take that as a compliment.  Yes. You feel there are certain  people that you have to interview.  If they don’t want to give you an  interview, you can’t, I feel, say no.  Like Lyndon Johnson’s first secretary, the one  who rode in the car with him on the campaigns.  I said, "There’s no other human being on earth  who knows what Lyndon Johnson is doing all   these hours driving back and forth across Texas. I don’t know what I have to do, but I have to get   him to tell me honestly about this thing." This raises another question   that I wanted to ask you. You’re interviewing all these people,   and in many cases, they must know that it’s not  good for them to tell you what you want to know.  In many cases, they tell you anyway. How do you get people to tell you things   that they know they shouldn’t tell you? You ask terrific questions. Sometimes   you’re sitting there and you know this person  doesn’t want to talk to you about what you   want to get out of them, like John Connally on  how Johnson used money to get political power.  I’m thinking, "But I’ve been through the notes. Connally collected the money and gave it out at   Johnson’s instructions, so he’s the only  guy who can tell me how Johnson did this,   how he judged who to give money to." Sometimes Johnson would write   on a request for money. If the guy asked for $1,500,   Johnson would write, "Okay, 1,500." Sometimes he’d write 500, sometimes he’d   write no, but sometimes he’d write, "No, never." I asked Connally what that meant, and he said,   "This guy was never going to  get money from Lyndon Johnson."  Then when you ask why he felt this way about  this particular congressman, that’s when the   really fascinating stories emerge. Before we get more into Johnson,   I want to first start with Moses. In the last decade or two,   people have been complaining that it’s become  too hard and too difficult to build things,   especially for the government to build things. If you look at the Second Avenue subway,   they’ve been building it for around 50 years. They’ve opened up a mile and a half.  It cost more than $4 billion. People have been saying,   "The Power Broker came out. It was an immensely influential book.  We were concerned about so much power  being centralized and delegated to one   person so they could build. We wanted to prevent that,   and so we made environmental review and land  use review and community boards and litigation."  People say, "We’ve overcorrected. We’ve  gone too far in the other direction."  What do you think of that? They also say that because   of all these safeguards, Robert Moses  could not operate in the same way today.  But the fact is, when Robert Moses  started, there were also safeguards.  People were also saying,  "You can’t build anything."  This was in the 1920s. People were saying,   "Government can’t build anything. There are too many blocks.  Nothing’s getting built. We need  highways. It’s the age of cars.  Everyone’s getting automobiles,  but we have the same old roads.  Nobody can build them because the property owners  don’t want the roads built through their land."  Robert Moses comes along, and all of a sudden  those things vanish because, despite all the   safeguards and everything else, he just builds. Doing The Power Broker, it was just fascinating   to me to see how he gets around everything. It doesn’t matter what it is.  He’s going to build a beach at Jones Beach. He sees it one day.  He says, "This is the  greatest beach I’ve ever seen.  It’s only 27 miles from New York City. If I can build a road out here, I will give   the people of New York City this great beach." But it seems impossible to build that road   because the property owners don’t want the  road going through their farms and property.  He basically says, "I’m going to build it." To watch him do it, to overcome each obstacle,   there are so many, and then all of a  sudden it’s open and you have Jones   Beach and you have it accessible to New York. It’s an act of political genius, and it’s also   an act of will: "I’m going to do it." That’s fascinating to learn about.  So you think today if there were a Moses-type  figure, they would figure out a way to work   around everything that’s been set up? The answer to that is, when Moses was   building, they were saying the same  thing. "Nobody’s ever going to build.  We need roads for the automobiles,  but they’d have to go through   dozens of farms, scores of properties. No one’s ever going to be able to do it."  But he comes along and does it. So today someone would come along and do it.  This, I think, is a profound question  for democracies: how do we end up in a   place which is not the extremes of ’50s or  ’60s Moses, but also not where we are now?  Where I live in California, we’ve spent, I  don’t know, $15 billion over the last decade.  We haven’t gotten a single new line  or single new mile of railway that   those $15 billion have been spent to build. Whereas in a different system… You could say China   today is like New York City in the ’40s and ’50s. They have a very Moses-type attitude and they   put up tens of thousands of miles of  railways over the last 10-20 years.  But of course, at the cost of similar amounts  of displacement of people and recklessness.  So how do we land in a good  spot between either extreme?  I’m not sure there is a good spot. What you just said is the situation.  To build anything on a large scale,  you’re confronted with dozens or   scores or perhaps hundreds of property  owners who don’t want it built there.  So the question is, how does anything get built? Then someone comes along and can do it.  When Robert Moses started, it seemed impossible,  actually impossible, to build roads out into   Long Island because the road would have to  cross scores of properties, most of whose   owners didn’t want the roads coming through. They had the power to stop them then because   he didn’t have the power of eminent domain. But Moses said basically, "I’m going to build it."  He would find a way to overcome each difficulty. What am I trying to say by that?  I’m trying to say that every once in a  while someone comes along who’s a genius,   if that’s the right word, at getting  big things built for the public.  Decades may pass when there’s no one like that. You say, "Everything’s stalled. Nothing big   is ever going to be built again." Then someone suddenly comes along   and all of a sudden things get built. That’s the nature of political genius.  I happen to be writing about two guys, Lyndon  Johnson and Robert Moses, Johnson with civil   rights and Moses with public works, where  people were saying, "You can’t do this."  But they did it. Correct me if I’m putting   words in your mouth, but if I may attempt an  interpretation of what you said, it sounds like   you think we need a little Moses today. A great insight. I sometimes wonder   about just what you said. The answer is, I certainly   don’t want someone who’s as ruthless and  disregarding public opinion as a Robert Moses.  But at the same time, you need someone who’s  going to find a way to get things built.  He’s going to have to find a way despite the  fact that so many people don’t want it built.  A lot of people who haven’t read the book  have this impression that you think everything   Moses did was bad, and that we need to make  sure that we can never have a Moses again.  So it’s interesting to hear you say  that we need a little Moses again.  When people say to me everything was bad that he  did, what I say is, "You didn’t read the book."  Because certainly the first parts of the book,  hundreds of pages, are about a young idealist   who sees this great need for recreation, for  beaches on Long Island for the city people,   and is going to find a way to make  them accessible to people in the city.  It’s an act of genius and willpower  the way he does it, and that’s great.  Now, does it evolve into where Moses listens  to nobody, and the only thing that matters is   what he wants to get built? It does evolve into that.  He does change. But the young Moses, the  idealist, before he’s building, is an expert   in the technicalities of civil service. He devotes all his energies to trying to   reform the civil service so that people get  promoted on merit instead of political pull.  He works so hard at that. You see a real idealism.  You see a real idealism in his early  works, when he says, "I want to make   these beaches accessible to New York." Now, does that evolve into "I think there   ought to be a highway here no matter  what anybody says, and no matter how   many thousands of people are in the way," like  the Cross Bronx Expressway, "I’ll evict them"?  It does. He changes. That to me is a big  part of the story of The Power Broker:   how this guy who’s in the beginning a young,  idealistic guy who wants to build to make   lives better for people, to give them access to  the ocean and beaches, changes into someone who   just wants to build because he thinks something  should be built no matter what anyone else says.  He’s going to do it no matter how many  hundreds, thousands of people he has to evict,   no matter how bad an idea it is,  like the Cross Bronx Expressway.  People are telling him not  to do that before he does it.  The minute this road opens, it’s  the world’s longest traffic jam.  Not thousands, but tens of thousands of  people were evicted, thrown out of their   homes by him without any relocation provisions. So in a way it’s a story of how you give somebody   power without the power, in a way — I don’t want  to use the word "corrupting" him — but hardening   him to anyone who opposes him, to any opposition. You start writing the book in ’66, ’67.  You’re writing it while Moses is losing power. His career is not over yet.  So the story changes while you’re writing it. I don’t know if you’ve talked about that,   but presumably the conclusion changes  because you don’t know whether he’s   going to lose that power or not when you start. That’s a great question. I watch that happen,   and I’m young. Whatever my age was,   I didn’t really know what I was doing. I watched him lose power, and I learned enough   about him to know how sad this was going to be. If I could think a moment, there's a moment that   this happened… Yeah… His office was still  up at the Triborough Bridge Authority.  When he was in power, I interviewed  him in that office several times.  You felt his power. You felt outside  there were all these people sitting   around waiting for his decisions. As soon as I finished, the secretary   would come in with a list of telephone  calls from people who had called wanting   something from him while I was talking to him. I remember I had one long interview with him.  Maybe it was my last one. By the time I finished, I realized   there had been no calls. The secretary had nothing to tell him.  So whatever you thought of Moses, you felt  the poignance of someone losing power.  That’s fascinating. That’s  what I was wondering about.  You couldn’t help feeling sad for him,  even though you knew what he had done.  You couldn’t help feeling, "Oh, this is,  in a way, tragic that no one’s calling   and asking him for a favor anymore." Did he realize that was happening?  I don’t think he really did. In a way, I’m sure he did.  But by that time he was so insulated. Whatever his age was, he was up in his 80s.  He was deaf. He still had at the Triborough  headquarters on Randall’s Island all these   Moses men who were loyal to him and treated  him with the same deference they always had.  He knew he wasn’t getting his projects done. But I know he felt he was just going to keep   pushing like he always did,  and he was going to win again.  The answer to your question is no, I  don’t think he did ever realize that.  In, I think, ’62, as you say, he tries to pull a  trick on Nelson Rockefeller that he had pulled on   countless previous mayors and governors, which is  to threaten to resign if he didn’t get his way.  Rockefeller says, "I regretfully  accept," and nothing happens.  That made me wonder as I was reading it. Could all those previous governors and mayors who   were getting threatened have done the same thing? Great question. Yeah, the answer is yes.  Well, you say, "could they  have done the same thing?"  In part, the answer is yes. They had the power to fire him.  He wasn’t an elected official. But there wasn’t really a possibility.  The answer to the question at the bottom is no,  they couldn’t, because he was simply too popular.  You couldn’t fire Robert Moses. That’s like firing some person   who was the idol of New York. But in addition, with his genius,   he had created, in all his different posts  — chairman of the State Power Authority,   chairman of Triborough Bridge Authority, Parks  Commissioner, Long Island Parks Commissioner,   Jones Beach Commissioner — such an interlocking  web that you couldn’t fire him from everything,   because the terms ended in different ways, and  some you didn’t have the power to fire him from.  He had really made it impossible. Well, almost impossible, because at the end,   if you wanted to do it, Rockefeller did it. But by that time,   cracks had appeared in the armor. I think for decades, the answer to your   question is you couldn’t do it. But then as he got older,   cracks appeared in the armor. If you wanted to brave criticism   in all the newspapers and public criticism and  everything else, you probably could have done it.  Which leads into the next  question I want to ask you.  You interviewed him seven times. The seventh time, you mentioned   your awareness of a donation that was made to his  commission by a millionaire whose golf course was   spared by the new route for his parkway. After that, he didn’t talk to you again.  If you had gotten an eighth interview with  Robert Moses, what is the one question   you would most want to ask him? Oh, God, what a great question.  Off the top of my head, if I only had  one question to ask him, I’d ask him,   "Did you realize you were changing?" That’s off the top... That’s   a great question you asked. But that’s the answer I’ll give for now.  That’s something I always  would like to have asked him.  Do you think he realized that he was changing? No. I think he felt from the beginning that he had   this vision to build roads here and parks there. That was the best thing to do.  It was going to get done, and it should get done. No matter how many hardships he had to inflict   on people, no matter how many thousands he  had to evict, no matter what he had to do,   he was going to get the roads built. You see this increasing ruthlessness,   this utter ruthlessness of him. If someone stood in his way, he was going to   find a way to remove that person as an obstacle. I’ll give you an example of that if you want.  There’s a politician in the  Bronx named Henry Epstein.  Henry Epstein is opposing  the Cross Bronx Expressway.  He’s saying to Robert Moses, "You’re putting  it right through a neighborhood where you   have to evict tens of thousands of people. You can just move it two blocks to the south,   and you only have to evict  a couple of hundred people."  Moses sets out to destroy Epstein, and basically  does, by making it known he’s having an affair.  If he can find a weakness in  somebody, that he has a mistress,   that he’s taking money or something, he’ll use it. He’ll use whatever he has to to get things done.  He learns that, in my opinion, by failing  to get things done when he’s very young.  He has things that he wants to  get done, and they don’t get done.  The awareness comes on him. We can see it in the book,   or in my learning about him. I try to show how he learns   that he has to find weaknesses in people. If he has a weakness, he’s going to use it.  He’s going to get things done. There’s a hardening, an increased   ruthlessness, where the only thing  that matters is to get the thing done.  Anyone who stands in his way is  going to get whatever it takes.  If Moses has to destroy him, he’ll destroy him. As you say, you’re writing not the history   of one man, but of an era in America. One of the most interesting things about   The Power Broker is, especially in the period in  which he’s able to accomplish so much so quickly,   what’s happening, and you talk  about this, is the Great Depression.  He’s hiring thousands of architects, tens  of thousands of linemen, for pennies on the   dollar to do big public works for the city. So I wonder how big a part of Moses’ early   achievements is just that the government,  because of the Great Depression, could   compete with the private sector for the top  talent and for lots and lots of labor working   24/7 through the winter, moving fast. Another great question. The answer is   that it played a big role. He needed architects for something.  I don’t remember what it is. It’s in The Power Broker.  They lined up on Fifth Avenue,  thousands of out-of-work architects   that he could hire for very low wages. But more than the wages, they were available,   because they didn’t have anything to do. He was able to hire so many people,   and hire and fire them in a ruthless  way, making the workmen work hard.  He could just fire them. It was the Depression. They   didn’t have other jobs to go to. He used that. Yes.  As somebody who has studied urban development  so deeply, here is one thing I’m curious about.  You look at the things that were built  at the beginning of the last century,   or before the beginning of the last century  — Grand Central Station and all the beautiful   architecture in New York — versus the things that  were built in the second half of the century.  They look a lot less beautiful. Behind everything — when Johnson   is talking to you, and he puts his arm around you,  and he leans into you — it’s not just the force of   his personality that he’s bringing to bear on you. Behind that personality, you know he has the   power to do things to you or for  you that you better be aware of.  Means of Ascent, the book about the election  with Coke Stevenson, the 1948 Senate election.  That is my favorite book perhaps ever. You paint such a compelling portrait of this   person, Coke Stevenson, governor of Texas. They called him Mr. Texas.  As you were writing his profile and  writing this book, did part of you wish   that he had won the Senate election? You couldn’t help feeling… I’ll   answer you directly. The answer is yes. I   think Coke Stevenson, although he was an  idealist, he knew how to get things done.  When he was governor of Texas,  he really accomplished things.  I think if he had gone to the Senate, he would  have been a great senator and accomplished things.  So you wish that he had won. You feel the tragedy that   he lost because of the way he lost. The thing about Coke Stevenson, he really   didn’t realize someone could do all the things  to him in the election that Lyndon Johnson did.  He didn’t come to grips with that. No, because Kennedy did not have the   overriding desire to change America. John Kennedy was utterly charming.  He was a good president. He was good in foreign policy,   where Johnson certainly was not. But what he did not have was this   vision, this desire to change  America that Lyndon Johnson had.  Lyndon Johnson comes back from his year teaching  the poor kids in Cotulla determined to change the   education system to help poor people more, to  do all these other things to help poor people.  That determination is  something that’s really unique.  It’s what made him domestically such a  great president, that we have all these   civil rights laws, these anti-poverty laws that  we wouldn’t have had without Lyndon Johnson.  His presidency ends in tragedy because  of foreign policy, because of Vietnam.  But he has this desire to get things done to  help people in America that’s almost unique.  You say, "Gee, he’s determined to do this." He’s going to find a way to do it.  You watch him doing it. Then you say, "He was doing it."  When his attention turns to Vietnam, everything  falls apart, and his presidency is ruined.  The things he started out to do domestically  don’t get done in the way he would have done them.  But he starts out after the election with  the education laws, with the anti-poverty   bills to change the country. He’s on his way to doing it.  That’s the great tragedy of Johnson and Vietnam. I wonder how much you think that is the fact   that they had a different constitution, that  they just had different reserves of energy.  Or do you think it was just  that their will was so strong?  I think it’s just their will. A lot of people have their energy.  When you see Robert Moses sleeping very little,  showing that he’d do anything to get his way,   to get things done, being tired or something  doesn’t even seem to figure into the equation.  Sometimes I’m looking at something —  I can’t remember one off the top of   my head — and you’ll say, "Johnson’s making  this call at 2:00 and 3:00 in the morning.  He’s up making these calls to get his way." In fact, there’s a funny anecdote.  Johnson calls one senator at 5:00 AM  to ask him for his vote on something,   and the senator says, "Oh, Lyndon, I was  just lying here waiting for your call."  So it’s their will. I want to ask you a  little bit about writing biography now.  One question I have is, you spend  5-10 years writing a single book.  Through that process, maybe  your editor and your wife are   the only people who have seen the manuscript. So how do you make sure you’re on the right track?  Because you’ve got to wait so long from when  you start to when you get public feedback.  How do you make sure that everything’s  going to hang together and you’re   pursuing the message the way you want to? Part of your question is, how do you be   sure you’re on the right track? The answer to that is you’re not.  But how do you try to stay on the right track? I do have a device for that.  Before I start a book — I learned this the hard  way with The Power Broker, because I didn’t do   it with The Power Broker — I think through  what I want the book to be, the whole book.  People say, "You mean you  think it through to the end?"  The answer is yes. Then you  say, "What is this book about?"  I sit at that desk sometimes for a long  time before I start writing, when I’m   thinking about the book, just asking myself in  one way or another, "What is this book about?"  You’ve got to get it down to one sentence. You say, "You can’t get it down to one sentence."  Then you say, "Yeah, but Bob, you learned  you better get it down to one sentence,   or three years from now you’re going to be writing  and you’re going to be saying, ‘What am I trying   to do?’" Before I start a book, I try to get it  down to a sentence or at most a paragraph and say,   "Really, what is this book about?" Over the 50 years that he has spent writing  about Lyndon Johnson, he has lived in the

He has sifted through millions of documents  in the Senate and presidential libraries
of the entire nation. He has chased down for
interviews everyone, from the former goon who  helped Johnson steal an election to the chauffeur

who understands Johnson’s aphorism:  "If you do everything, you’ll win."
Mr. Caro, it is such a huge  honor to have you on the show.
It’s great to be here. My first question is what
I hinted at in the introduction. How much do you see yourself
represented in Johnson or in Moses? Is part of the reason you’re able to

You say they’d do anything to win. That’s part of their greatness.

There was this row of file  cabinets against the wall.
I’m sitting there day after day  going through these documents.
Occasionally I’d come across a note that  Robert Moses wrote, and I realized I’m
following the same path he was. It’s fascinating, actually.
Obviously, not all the qualities. But the quality I’m referring to

You refuse to leave a stone unturned. So there is a relentlessness that
you share with these subjects. I’m going to take that as a compliment.
Yes. You feel there are certain  people that you have to interview.

Like Lyndon Johnson’s first secretary, the one  who rode in the car with him on the campaigns.
